description: Meet Phoenix Pavillion (Matthew Wong, Dorothy Wong, and Michelle Koh)! 🚀✨ We’re competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge under the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" theme. Our mission? Creating an interactive children’s storybook that shares the untold stories of NASA’s historic equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars! 🌕🔴
summary:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive digital storybook introducing kids aged 4–8 to NASA’s dormant and deep-space hardware through character-driven video storytelling.
While young learners mostly hear about active missions, our book brings four historic off-world artifacts back to life:
•	Refly (Apollo Mirror): Bounces laser beams back to Earth from the Moon without batteries.
•	Soie (Sojourner Rover): Climbed Martian rocks to uncover clues of ancient water.
•	Pi-10 (Pioneer 10): Crossed the Asteroid Belt, slingshotted past Jupiter, and carries humanity’s golden plaque into deep space.
•	Kepi (Kepler Space Telescope): Discovered over 2,600 exoplanets by watching dips in starlight.
Built in Canva, our "Tap-to-Watch" interface lets pre-readers tap any character's name to launch a YouTube animated episode. Using Canva, Google Vids, and Gemini, we translated complex astrophysics into intuitive visual stories.
By offering free, browser-based STEM education for early learners, our project supports UN SDG 4 (Quality Education)—promoting inclusive early childhood learning—and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) by removing costly software or hardware barriers so children everywhere can explore space history.
details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive digital children’s storybook designed for kids aged 4–8 that brings NASA’s dormant and deep-space hardware back to life through playful, character-driven video storytelling.

Rather than presenting dense historical text, the storybook turns four iconic off-world artifacts into relatable, voiced guides:

  • Refly (Apollo Retroreflector Array): Shares how it still bounces laser beams back to Earth from the Moon without using any batteries or electrical power.
  • Soie (Mars Pathfinder Sojourner Rover): Recounts how its six tiny wheels climbed Martian rocks and analyzed pebbles to prove ancient water once flowed on Mars.
  • Pi-10 (Pioneer 10 Space Probe): Tells the story of navigating the Asteroid Belt, slingshotting past Jupiter, and carrying humanity’s golden plaque toward the stars.
  • Kepi (Kepler Space Telescope): Explains how watching tiny dips in starlight revealed over 2,600 hidden exoplanets before retiring in solar orbit.

Built in Canva, the storybook features a simple "Tap-to-Watch" interface tailored for pre-readers and early readers. Children explore an illustrated cosmic map of the Moon, Mars, and deep space; tapping any character's name opens a linked YouTube video playing their short animated episode (70–120 seconds), complete with expressive voiceovers, sound effects, and visual metaphors.

What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Because it runs through Canva and YouTube in any standard web browser on phones, tablets, or computers, families and classrooms need no special hardware, app installations, or paid software.
  • Pre-Reader Friendly: Relying on tap-activated animated videos and lively narration allows children as young as 4 years old to navigate and learn independently without needing strong reading skills.
  • Scientifically Accurate yet Intuitive: Complex aerospace concepts—such as Lunar Laser Ranging, rocker-bogie suspension, gravitational assists, and transit photometry—are translated into concrete visual comparisons (such as playing laser catch or watching a moth fly across a porch light) while maintaining strict historical and technical accuracy.

What is the intended impact of the project?

While young space enthusiasts often hear about active missions like Perseverance or the James Webb Space Telescope, the pioneering hardware that made modern exploration possible is frequently overlooked. Through Abandoned but not Forgotten, we aim to:

  • Spark Early STEM Curiosity: Introduce preschool and early elementary learners to planetary science, robotics, and astrophysics at an age when imagination is at its peak.
  • Honor Space Exploration Heritage: Help children see "discarded" spacecraft not as space trash, but as enduring monuments of human curiosity—many of which are still actively contributing to science or traveling through the cosmos today.
  • Advance UN Sustainable Development Goals: Directly support SDG 4 (Quality Education) by promoting inclusive early childhood STEM learning, and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) by making engaging space education freely available to children everywhere regardless of economic background.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Our team combined accessible no-code creative platforms and AI tools to maximize visual storytelling and cross-device compatibility:

  • Canva: Used to illustrate the custom characters (Refly, Soie, Pi-10, Kepi), design the interactive storybook pages, and embed clickable character name hyperlinks.
  • Google Vids: Used to assemble, animate, and edit the short character video episodes with dynamic visual effects and pacing suited for young learners.
  • YouTube: Used to host and stream the individual animated episodes seamlessly when children tap a character's name in the storybook.
  • Gemini: Used to brainstorm age-appropriate narrative hooks, draft engaging character scripts for 4–8 year olds, and distill complex NASA mission logs into accurate, kid-friendly explanations.
  • NASA Open Data & Mission Archives: Referenced the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, Mars Pathfinder Mission Logs, Pioneer 10 Overview, and the NASA Exoplanet Archive to verify mission timelines, engineering mechanics, and scientific discoveries.

How is your project creative?

  • First-Person Artifact Storytelling: Instead of a third-person documentary or encyclopedia entry, each piece of hardware speaks in the first person with its own distinct personality—turning cold metal, glass prisms, and solar panels into warm, memorable friends.
  • Visual Metaphors for Astrophysics: We bridged the gap between early childhood cognition and space science by turning abstract physics into everyday play (e.g., framing Lunar Laser Ranging as a nightly game of "laser catch" across 238,900 miles, and comparing exoplanet transits to a moth passing a lamp).
  • Hybrid Storybook-to-Video Experience: Combining the tactile, self-paced feel of a picture book in Canva with clickable YouTube video episodes creates an interactive multimedia experience without requiring complex app development.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Target Age Group & Attention Span (Ages 4–8): Young children have developing literacy skills and shorter attention spans. We kept every video episode tight (under 90 seconds), prioritized audio-visual storytelling over walls of text, and made the tap targets large and intuitive.
  • Balance Between Whimsy and Accuracy: When writing for young kids, it is easy to oversimplify until facts become inaccurate. We carefully verified every scientific detail—such as the Moon's 1.5-inch annual drift, Sojourner's 83-sol survival versus its 7-sol design life, and Kepler's Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit—so children learn real science from day one.
  • Ease of Distribution & Device Compatibility: Knowing that parents and teachers use a wide mix of smartphones, tablets, Chromebooks, and classroom projectors, we intentionally chose a lightweight web-based Canva + YouTube workflow so anyone can open and share the storybook with a single link.
